01The answer on one page

One scoring rule turned a timing change into a trap.

Whathappened

4.2 cut the ping wait from 90 to 60 seconds, and missed pings jumped from 2% to 23%. The code scores a miss exactly like a "no", and only a "yes" earns points back. Four responders sank to zero and stopped being asked.

Whynobody caught it

Acceptance was back to 75% by September, because the four weren't asked any more and the other twelve absorbed their work. There was no brief, no experiment and no owner watching.

Costto the business

At the peak, 1 in 5 callouts found nobody. Tickets rose 4×. A quarter of the roster sat idle while the rest carried 27% more, and Rook bills per active responder.

Fixwhat I'd do

Keep the 60-second wait and the proximity change. Stop counting a miss as a no, give quiet responders a way back, show Kip why, and make "system health" a release gate.

51→6
pings a week to the quiet four
Decision needed

Approve a two-week staged rollout in two areas, starting with Eastgate, behind a flag, with guardrails at both ends and a rollback trigger. The code change is small. The risk is shipping it the way 4.2 shipped.

08Keeping it from happening again

A brief that reads well isn't a brief that ships safely.

My review-checklist skill checks every brief the same way and quotes the line behind each verdict. It runs on its own every Monday at 08:12. Checks 7 and 8 are new, and they're the ones 4.2 needed.

1Owner namedA person, not a role.
2Success measureSomething you can count.
3Scope stays boundedSame ask from start to end.
4Problem before fixWho has it comes first.
5EvidenceA number or quote, with its source.
6A specific personA real user, and what changes for them.
7 · NewSystem healthLoops have a brake. Load is guarded at both ends. Everyone has a way back.
8 · NewTested before, watched afterOld → new values, a replay or staged rollout, a rollback trigger, a named person on week one.

North star

Share of callouts with a yes within X minutes. Until answer time is tracked: callouts nobody took, back to 5.5% or below.

Guardrails, both ends

No available responder idle for 5+ days. Nobody above 1.5× their usual pings for a week.

Rollback trigger (proposed)

Callouts nobody took above 8% for 3 days in a test area, or a guardrail broken for a week: the flag goes off.

What I'm taking away

The system didn't need a hero. It needed a brake, a guardrail and someone watching.

M1 · Onboard

Brief Claude once in CLAUDE.md, and it knows the job every session.

M2 · Listen

Ask for counts and quotes. Interviews and tickets were different people.

M3 · Verify

See the rows and check twice. The average hid four people.

M4 · Inspect

Ask what the code doesn't do. Nothing gave points back.

M5 · Prototype

Brief, build, then argue with it. My pushback made the model honest.

M6 · Automate

Write the check once, and let it run every Monday.

Appendix A1
Why the dashboard looked fine

The average hid four people.

Acceptance: 75.8% → 54.3% → 75.2%. By early September the headline number was back to normal, because the people missing pings were no longer being asked.

Coverage came back by overloading the rest. The other twelve went from about 10 to 13 pings each a week. The Gale hit 15–20. Tired responders miss pings too, which feeds the same loop from the other end.

Lesson: every success metric needs a guardrail on the spread, not just the average.

Appendix A2
Options considered · same pings, different rules

One rule change does most of the work.

✕ Roll back 4.2

Responders covering wide areas asked for the proximity change. A rollback swaps one angry group for another and leaves the trap in the code.

✕ Score recovery only

Too slow. The four end at 0.23–0.35, still 10 minutes behind.

✓ A miss isn't a no

The four stay at 0.76–0.84, about 3 minutes behind. The replay understates it, because they'd also have got more pings.

✓ Plus a way back

On launch day the four are still at 0. Only the 5-day check-in gets them asked again.
